        "title": "Proper acceleration of a massive worldline and its agreement with the acceleration of an observer congruence",
        "statement": "Let c > 0 and let x: I -> A be a C^2 future timelike worldline with four-velocity U = dx/dtau and four-acceleration A = dU/dtau (def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration), so that eta(U,U) = -c^2 and eta(U,A) = 0 pointwise, and A(tau) is spacelike whenever it is nonzero (thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition (a),(b)). (a) Definition. The proper acceleration of x at the parameter value tau is the real number a(tau) := sqrt(eta(A(tau),A(tau))), the nonnegative square root of def-rational-power. This is well defined for every tau in I: if A(tau) = 0 then eta(A,A) = 0, and if A(tau) is nonzero then it is spacelike and eta(A,A) > 0 (def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors); in both cases the argument of the square root is nonnegative, so a(tau) is a nonnegative real number. With the SI coordinate and unit conventions of def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions, in which x^0 = c t with t in seconds and the spatial coordinates are in metres while eta has the dimensionless matrix diag(-1,1,1,1) in an inertial chart, the components of A carry the unit metre per second squared and eta(A,A) carries the unit (metre per second squared)^2, so a carries the unit metre per second squared. The worldline is uniformly accelerated when a is constant on I. (b) Agreement with the acceleration of a congruence. Let Omega be a nonempty open subset of A and let n: Omega -> V be an observer congruence with acceleration field a_cg := nabla_n n, where nabla is the flat covariant derivative of def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space (def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics (b)). If x is a flow line of n and U = c n along x, then A = c^2 a_cg along x, and consequently a = c^2 sqrt(eta(a_cg,a_cg)) along x: the proper acceleration is c^2 times the magnitude of the congruence acceleration. In particular the proper acceleration of a congruence worldline is determined by the congruence field alone, and such a worldline is uniformly accelerated exactly when eta(a_cg,a_cg) is constant along it. (c) Reading and scope. This item defines a quantity of the model and fixes its name, its unit and its physical reading. The model reads a(tau) as the magnitude that an ideal accelerometer carried along the worldline would register at tau; this ideal-instrument identification is adopted with the model in the same sense as the framework's ideal-clock reading of proper time and is not derived here. No accelerometer response law, calibration, frequency dependence, force law or interaction is specified or asserted; the definition asserts nothing about which bodies follow which worldlines; no measurement outcome and no statistical, uncertainty or empirical claim is made. No choice principle is used.",
        "strategy": "Definition with its well-definedness and its unit and congruence clauses justified by the cited suppliers. (a) A is continuous because x is C^2 (def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline, def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration (b)); eta(A,A) is the sum of products of continuous component functions in any inertial chart (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart, thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions); eta(A,A) >= 0 pointwise by thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition (b) together with the classification of nonzero spacelike vectors by def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors. Hence sqrt(eta(A,A)) is well defined for every tau as the nonnegative real whose square is eta(A,A) (def-rational-power). Units are read off directly from def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions, which lists the unit metre per second squared for the four-acceleration and the dimensionless matrix diag(-1,1,1,1) for eta in an inertial chart.         "statement": "Let $\\Omega$ be a nonempty open subset of affine Minkowski space $A$, $c>0$, and let $n:\\Omega\\to V$ be a $C^1$ future unit timelike field, $\\eta(n,n)=-1$. Here $h$ is $C^1$ and $a,\\theta$ are continuous. The rest projection $h(v):=v+\\eta(n,v)n$ is as in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]](c). For $C^1$ fields and tensors define\n$$(L_nh)_{ab}:=n^c\\partial_ch_{ab}+h_{cb}\\partial_an^c+h_{ac}\\partial_bn^c.$$\nThese first-order coordinate formulas transform tensorially under affine inertial chart changes and agree, on smooth fields, with [[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]], [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]] and the ordinary smooth Lie derivative. Say the $C^1$ field is Born rigid when $L_nh=0$; the identity $L_nh=2\\theta$ makes this equivalent to $\\theta=0$.\n(a) Let $J$ be a nonempty open interval, $B\\subseteq\\mathbb R^3$ a nonempty open set, and $\\Phi:J\\times B\\to\\Omega$ an injective $C^2$ immersion with $\\partial_s\\Phi=n(\\Phi)$. Put $e_I:=\\partial_{\\xi^I}\\Phi$, $I=1,2,3$, and $G_{IJ}(s,\\xi):=h(e_I,e_J)$ at $\\Phi(s,\\xi)$. Then $n,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are linearly independent, $G$ is symmetric positive definite at every point, and its entries are $C^1$. Thus for each $s$ it is a $C^1$ positive-definite material metric on $B$. If $n$ and $\\Phi$ are smooth, $G$ is a smooth Riemannian metric, as in the original smooth branch.\n(b) For all $I,J$,\n$$\\partial_sG_{IJ}=(L_nh)(e_I,e_J)=2\\theta(e_I,e_J),\\qquad\\partial_\\tau G_{IJ}=2c\\theta(e_I,e_J),$$\nwhere $\\tau=s/c$ is the proper-time parameter along each flow line, whose four-velocity is $cn$. The smooth Born-rigid branch and its original conclusions are included.\n(d) This is a local statement about the given family and its material metric. Integrating the material metric at a common flow parameter gives an internal label-space length; it does not identify that length with a finite endpoint distance on a single observer's orthogonal simultaneity hyperplane without an additional argument.         "statement": "Worked computation in the Rindler chart of pthm-sr-rindler-horizons-and-radar. The future null line from e_- of constant V has V = -rho_0, and it meets rho = 2rho_0 at the Rindler time theta_m = log 2; using sinh(log 2) = 3/4 and cosh(log 2) = 5/4 (thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives, thm-natural-logarithm-laws) the reflection event is q_m = x^{-1}(3rho_0/2, 5rho_0/2, 0, 0), and the return event is e_+ = x^{-1}(rho_0 sinh(2log 2), rho_0 cosh(2log 2), 0, 0) = x^{-1}(15rho_0/8, 17rho_0/8, 0, 0) at Rindler time theta(e_+) = 2 log 2. The two worldlines rho = rho_0 and rho = 2rho_0 are at rest distance rho_0 in the slice theta = log 2; since e > 2 gives log 2 < 1 (cor-two-less-than-e-less-than-three, thm-natural-logarithm-laws), the radar distance is strictly smaller than the rest distance. This definition introduces the framework's experimental-interface vocabulary; it selects no experiment, records no value and asserts no comparison.\n\n**(a) Run descriptions.** A *run description* is a finite tuple $D=(d_1,\\dots,d_r)$ whose entries are framework objects of the following kinds, each declared with its domain and regularity as specified by the cited item, together with the frame, observer, event or unit convention required for a numerical reading where such a reading is used: a point of the affine Minkowski space $A$ (an event, [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]); a vector of $V$ of declared causal character ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]); a future timelike worldline together with its proper-time function ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]], [[def-sr-proper-time]]); a future unit timelike vector or a smooth observer congruence ([[def-sr-chart-tetrad-and-congruence-distinction]]); a future null wave covector with its affine phase ([[def-sr-affine-phase-and-wave-covector]]); a radar time or radar distance assigned by the operational radar protocol ([[def-sr-operational-radar-protocol]]); an observer angular frequency ([[def-sr-null-wave-covector-and-observer-frequency]]); an observer energy, spatial momentum, kinetic energy or invariant mass ([[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]); and a real parameter vector in a declared subset of $\\mathbb R^m$ with declared units. A *calibration declaration* is a tuple $C=(Z,c,\\delta,h)$ with $c:Z\\to\\mathbb R^d$, $\\delta:Z\\to[0,\\infty)^d$ and $h$ a condition annotation; it declares that for every $z\\in Z$ obtained under the condition annotated by $h$, the value of the declared quantity lies in the closed box $\\prod_j[c_j(z)-\\delta_j(z),\\,c_j(z)+\\delta_j(z)]$ in the declared units.         "statement": "## Setup\n\nThe experiment used $^7\\mathrm{Li}^+$ ions from a Penning ion gauge source, accelerated to $58.6\\,\\mathrm{MeV/u}$ and stored in the ESR at nominal $\\beta=0.338$. About $10^7$ to $10^8$ ions were stored, with an estimated metastable fraction below $1\\%$. The metastable $3S_1$ lifetime was $15$–$30\\,\\mathrm{s}$ in the ring, compared with $50\\,\\mathrm{s}$ in vacuum. The Lambda system used the transitions $3S_1(F=3/2)\\to3P_2(F=5/2)$ and $3S_1(F=5/2)\\to3P_2(F=5/2)$. Parallel and antiparallel beams near $386\\,\\mathrm{nm}$ and $780\\,\\mathrm{nm}$ addressed its two legs; an additional $780\\,\\mathrm{nm}$ beam repumped ions into the system.\n\n## Procedure\n\nThe parallel beam was generated by doubling a $772\\,\\mathrm{nm}$ Ti:Sa laser locked to an iodine marker previously calibrated with a frequency comb against a rubidium clock. The antiparallel diode laser was offset-locked to a rubidium reference, with a $600\\,\\mathrm{MHz}$ tuning range. Polarization-maintaining fibers transported the beams. Motorized stages controlled angles and positions to $20\\,\\mu\\mathrm{rad}$ and $50\\,\\mu\\mathrm{m}$; scrapers established laser/ion overlap within $80\\,\\mu\\mathrm{rad}$. Photomultipliers counted fluorescence in four successive $100\\,\\mu\\mathrm{s}$ configurations: both excitation beams, antiparallel only, parallel only, and neither. Dark counts were subtracted, then the separate-beam background was subtracted from the both-beam spectrum. Optical-optical double resonance selected ions for which both Lambda legs were resonant at the same velocity. To compensate metastable depletion, an $81$-point scan was paused after $69$ points for injection and cooling. Figure 2 shows an example averaged over $44$ scans, with $49\\,\\mathrm{MHz}$ laboratory linewidth and $35\\,\\mathrm{MHz}$ rest-frame linewidth. The authors fitted $40$ spectra with Lorentzians on linear backgrounds and formed a weighted average. Raw count tables, fit weights, a covariance matrix and a complete likelihood are not published in this report.\n\n## Observations\n\nTable I gives the frequency estimates, in MHz, $\\nu_1=546455143.0$, $\\nu_2=546474960.7$, $\\nu_a=384225534.98$ and $\\nu_p=777210326.98$. The rest-frame inputs $\\nu_1,\\nu_2$ come from earlier measurements cited as references 21–22; those papers were not retrieved or read here. Equation (4) reports $\\epsilon=\\sqrt{\\nu_a\\nu_p/(\\nu_1\\nu_2)}-1=(1.5\\pm2.3)\\times10^{-9}$ at nominal $\\beta=0.338$. The inferred Gouy correction for each laser was $0.44\\pm1.0\\,\\mathrm{MHz}$, from experimentally validated numerical simulation using measured beam parameters. The authors reported no significant residual asymmetry; simulated background linearization was assigned $0.5\\,\\mathrm{MHz}$. The excess linewidth, about five times the expected width, was attributed mainly to drift-induced fluorescence. The $0.6\\,\\mathrm{MHz}$ statistical entry comes from the weighted analysis of forty fitted spectra, not forty independent raw clock readings.         "statement": "Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), let $\\theta_0\\in I$, and let $f:I\\to\\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on $I$ in the sense that $f$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ and $f'$ is continuous on $I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]). Assume $f(\\theta_0)=0$ and that $f'(\\theta)\\ge m>0$ for every $\\theta\\in I$. Let a recorded scalar $\\hat y\\in\\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\\hat y|\\le s$ with $s\\ge0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), and let a separately specified calibration-error model bound be $|y-\\hat y|\\le\\delta$ with $\\delta\\ge0$ for a value $y$ assigned to the same quantity. If a model requires $y=f(\\theta)$ for some $\\theta\\in I$, then every $\\theta\\in I$ compatible with those two simultaneous bounds satisfies $$|\\theta-\\theta_0|\\le\\frac{s+\\delta}{m};$$ equivalently, if a proposed $\\theta$ violates this bound, then the specified model-plus-error-bound pair is incompatible with the premises.         "statement": "For $z\\in[-1,1]$ define the real polynomial $P_l(z)=\\pi^{-1}\\int_0^\\pi\\bigl[z+i\\sqrt{1-z^2}\\,\\cos\\theta\\bigr]^l\\,d\\theta$, $l\\in\\mathbb N_0$. Then $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$ with $|P_l(z)|\\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, $P_l(1)=1$, and for $|q|<1$ the series $\\sum_{l\\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-1,1]$ with $$(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\\sum_{l=0}^{\\infty}q^lP_l(z),$$ where the branch is the analytic square root equal to $1$ at $q=0$ ([[def-series-of-real-functions]], [[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-function-series]]). Consequently, for $r>|y|$ with $n=x/|x|$ and $N\\in\\mathbb N_0$, $\\bigl|\\,|x-y|^{-1}-\\sum_{l=0}^{N}|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(n\\cdot y/|y|)\\bigr|\\le|y|^{N+1}|x|^{-N-2}(1-|y|/|x|)^{-1}$, uniformly on $|y|\\le a<r$ (with $y=0$ interpreted by the zero higher terms), and after integrating against an $L^1$ source the corresponding multipole expansion converges with that error times its $L^1$ norm.         "statement": "Let $c>0$, $0\\le v_*<c$, and $z:\\mathbb R\\to\\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\\in\\mathbb R^3\\times\\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\\{(x,t):x\\ne z(t)\\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\\kappa=1-n\\cdot\\beta$, its derivatives are $\\partial_t s=1/\\kappa$ and $\\nabla_xs=-n/(c\\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\\le\\kappa\\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.",
        "strategy": "The ordinary vector FTC and integral triangle inequality give $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\\le v_*|s_2-s_1|$. For fixed $x$ put $g_x(s)=s+|x-z(s)|/c$. It is continuous and for $s_2>s_1$ satisfies $g_x(s_2)-g_x(s_1)\\ge(1-v_*/c)(s_2-s_1)>0$. Consequently $g_x(s)\\to\\pm\\infty$ as $s\\to\\pm\\infty$; IVT and strict monotonicity give a unique solution of $g_x(s)=t$. Since $g_x(s)\\ge s$, $s\\le t$, and equality is equivalent to $x=z(t)$. On $D$ the root has $r>0$. Continuity of $z$ makes $D$ open. Near any root on $D$, $F(x,t,s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ has precisely the regularity of $z$, because the Euclidean norm is smooth away from zero. Its $s$ derivative is $-\\kappa$, bounded away from zero. Apply the parametrized implicit-function theorem with its actual $C^1$ hypothesis first, or with $C^k$ when $z$ is $C^k$; global uniqueness glues these local maps. Differentiating $F=0$ gives the two stated formulas. Repeat for every finite $k$ in the smooth case. Do not infer $C^3$ from $C^1$, and do not exclude an observation point merely because the trajectory visits it at a different time. The exact non-improvement witness is a small uniformly subluminal $z(s)=(\\epsilon\\chi(s)|s|^{3/2},0,0)$ with smooth compact cutoff $\\chi=1$ near zero. At a distant positive axial point $L>\\sup|z|$, the retardation map is $g(s)=s+(L-\\epsilon\\chi(s)|s|^{3/2})/c$, $C^1$ but not $C^2$ at zero. A $C^2$ inverse near $t=L/c$, whose derivative is nonzero, would make $g$ $C^2$ by the inverse-function theorem, a contradiction."

        "statement": "Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Here locally absolutely continuous means that each real entry restricted to every compact interval $[a,b]\\subseteq[0,\\infty)$ satisfies the finite disjoint-interval condition of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]: for every $\\epsilon>0$ there is $\\delta>0$ such that $\\sum_\\ell(v_\\ell-u_\\ell)<\\delta$ implies $\\sum_\\ell|K_{jk}(v_\\ell)-K_{jk}(u_\\ell)|<\\epsilon$ for every finite family with disjoint interiors. $K\\prime$ denotes the almost-everywhere derivative, with any measurable zero extension on its null exceptional set. Here $\\operatorname{PV}\\int_{\\mathbb R}F(\\xi)/(\\xi-\\omega)d\\xi$ means $\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\lim_{\\eta\\downarrow0}(\\int_{\\omega-R}^{\\omega-\\eta}+\\int_{\\omega+\\eta}^{\\omega+R})F(\\xi)/(\\xi-\\omega)d\\xi$; the tails converge absolutely, so the choice of centering at infinity does not change the limit. For an instantaneous real response matrix $\\chi_\\infty\\in\\mathbb R^{d\\times d}$ define the total transfer function $\\chi_{\\mathrm{total}}:=\\chi_\\infty+\\chi$; the formulas then apply to $\\chi_{\\mathrm{total}}-\\chi_\\infty=\\chi$; the scalar case is $d=1$. Along the real boundary the same theorem in the real parameter and the same majorant give the continuous derivative $\\chi\\prime(\\omega)=\\int_0^\\infty isk(s)e^{i\\omega s}ds$.\nFor fixed $z\\ne0$, the real and imaginary parts of $g(s):=e^{izs}$ are $C^1$ on each $[0,N]$, hence absolutely continuous by [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]]. Apply [[thm-integration-by-parts-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]] separately to $(k,\\operatorname{Re}g)$ and $(k,\\operatorname{Im}g)$ and combine the real identities to get\n$$\\int_0^N k(s)e^{izs}ds=\\frac{k(N)e^{izN}-k(0)}{iz}-\\frac1{iz}\\int_0^N k\\prime(s)e^{izs}ds.$$\nThis is Lebesgue integration by parts for AC functions, not the ordinary everywhere-differentiable Riemann theorem.         "statement": "Let (V,eta) be a 4-dimensional Lorentz vector space (def-lorentz-form-and-inertia) with a chosen time orientation C^+ (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets), and let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model). (a) A linear Lorentz map is a linear map L: V -> V such that eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V. The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted O(V,eta). (b) If (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is an ordered eta-orthonormal basis of V (lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis), eta_0 := diag(-1,1,1,1) is the matrix of eta in it, and M is the matrix of L in that basis (def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map), then L is a linear Lorentz map if and only if M^T eta_0 M = eta_0; every linear Lorentz map is a linear isomorphism, and the condition does not depend on the eta-orthonormal basis used. (c) A linear Lorentz map L is proper if det L = +1 and orthochronous if L(C^+) = C^+; the set of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps is denoted SO^+(V,eta). O(V,eta) is called the (full) Lorentz group of (V,eta) and SO^+(V,eta) the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; that these are groups under composition is proved in lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure.         "statement": "Let (V,eta) be the Lorentz vector space with time orientation C^+ and let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model. If beta is the parameter of B(beta), then beta = tanh r for a unique rapidity r in R, and collinear rapidities add. (ii) SO^+(V,eta) is a subgroup of O(V,eta), which is a subgroup of GL(V); every passive boost B(beta) and every spatial rotation of the frame (extended by fixing e_0) belongs to SO^+(V,eta).         "statement": "Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula.",

        "statement": "Let x:[a,b]->A, a<b, be a piecewise C^1 curve in the sense of def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline, with a finite partition a=s_0<...<s_m=b, C^1 on each open piece and finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of each piece. (b) Every coordinate derivative is absolutely improperly Riemann integrable; its signed improper integral equals the corresponding endpoint increment. Since y0'>=|z'|>=0, their squared values lie between 0 and (y0')^2, giving 0<=f<=y0' by the nonnegative square-root order. Hence u |-> sqrt(g_x(u)) is continuous on I (thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives, thm-composition-of-continuous-functions) and Riemann integrable on every compact subinterval of I (thm-continuous-implies-integrable). For s_0, s in I the proper time from s_0 to s is tau(s) := c^{-1} integral_{s_0}^{s} sqrt(-eta(x'(u),x'(u))) du, the integral being the oriented integral of def-oriented-integral; explicitly, for a < b in I, tau(b) - tau(a) = c^{-1} integral_a^b sqrt(-eta(x'(u),x'(u))) du, and changing the base point s_0 changes tau by an additive constant. tau depends on the parametrized history of x and on the parameter values; its invariance under increasing C^1 reparametrizations is proved in lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance.         "statement": "Work in the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (A,V,eta,C^+) (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) with its inertial atlas (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas) and the canonical identification T_pA = V (lem-tangent-space-of-affine-minkowski-space-is-v). The following objects are defined and are, in general, different objects. (a) Chart and inertial chart. A chart of the model is a diffeomorphism u: U -> u(U) from a nonempty open subset U of A onto an open subset of R^4 (def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds, def-smooth-manifold), written with components (u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3). An inertial chart (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart) is the global chart x(p) = E^{-1}(p-o) of an inertial frame (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3). A general chart need not be inertial: if x is an inertial chart and N: x(U) -> R^4 is a diffeomorphism onto its image which is not the restriction of an affine map, then u := N o x is a chart that is not inertial, because if u were the inertial chart of a frame then x o u^{-1} = N^{-1} would be affine by lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz and hence N = (N^{-1})^{-1} would be affine as the inverse of an affine bijection, a contradiction; the map N(y) = (y^0, y^1 + (y^0)^2, y^2, y^3) on R^4 is an explicit example. (b) Tetrad at an event and tetrad field. A tetrad at p in A is an ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) of V with eta(e_a,e_b) = diag(-1,1,1,1)_{ab} and e_0 future (e_0 in C^+); this is an inertial frame's basis without an origin and without the orientation condition. A tetrad field on a nonempty open subset Omega of A is a tuple (E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3) of smooth vector fields on Omega (def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space, type (1,0)) whose values at every p form a tetrad at p; it is observer-adapted when E_0 = U/c for a prescribed future timelike worldline or congruence. (c) Observer congruence. An observer congruence on a nonempty open subset Omega of A is a smooth vector field n: Omega -> V with eta(n,n) = -1 and n(p) in C^+ for all p; its observers are its maximal integral curves (def-integral-curve-of-a-vector-field, thm-unique-maximal-integral-curve-through-each-point), each of which is a future timelike worldline (def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline); n is nowhere zero because it is unit. Completeness of the integral curves, a global product structure of Omega and global synchronization are not asserted. (d) Adapted chart. For a congruence n on Omega, an n-adapted chart is a chart (u^0,u^1,u^2,u^3): U -> R^4 with U a nonempty open subset of Omega whose spatial coordinates u^1,u^2,u^3 are constant along every integral curve of n contained in U; no global adapted chart is asserted, and u^0 is not required to be affine. (e) Distinctions. A chart need not be inertial (a); a chart need not be n-adapted for any congruence; a tetrad field is not in general the coordinate frame of a chart: if (E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3) is the coordinate frame of a chart (v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3), i.e. E_a = partial/partial v^a, then [E_a,E_b] = 0 for all a,b (def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields, prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket), so a tetrad field whose members do not commute pairwise is not a coordinate frame; no converse is claimed here. A congruence need not be a coordinate flow, and its pointwise rest spaces need not assemble into hypersurfaces; that integrability question is decided below on this page. In an inertial chart the coordinate frame is simultaneously an inertial frame's basis, a constant tetrad field and the congruence of stationary observers, but the four notions are distinct in general.",
        "strategy": "Definition item; well-definedness and consistency obligations. (ii) Tetrads exist at every point by lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis and lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist; a tetrad field is componentwise smooth in an inertial chart (def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space).         "title": "The flat covariant derivative on affine Minkowski space and fields along curves",
        "statement": "Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the affine Minkowski space with tangent spaces canonically identified with V, and let Omega be a nonempty open subset of A. (a) Vector fields. For smooth vector fields X,Y on Omega (def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space) define the covariant derivative of Y in the direction X at p by (nabla_X Y)(p) := (d/dt)|_{t=0} Y(p + t X(p)); in the inertial chart x of any inertial frame this is (nabla_X Y)^a = X^b partial_b Y^a. The value does not depend on the inertial chart: for another inertial chart x' = Lambda x + b one has partial'_a = (Lambda^{-1})^b_a partial_b and Y'^a = Lambda^a_b Y^b (thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation), and Lambda is constant, so (Lambda^{-1})^a_c X'^b partial'_b Y'^c = X^b partial_b Y^a. nabla_X Y is again a smooth vector field. (b) Covector and general tensor fields. For a smooth covector field alpha set (nabla_X alpha)(Y) := X(alpha(Y)) - alpha(nabla_X Y); for a type (r,s) tensor field T define nabla_X T by the derivation rule on the evaluation of T on smooth vector and covector fields, subtracting the covariant derivative of each vector argument and also subtracting the covariant derivative of each covector argument; Precisely, for $T:(V^*)^r\\times V^s\\to\\mathbb R$, $(\\nabla_XT)(\\alpha_1,\\ldots,\\alpha_r;Y_1,\\ldots,Y_s)=X[T(\\alpha_1,\\ldots,\\alpha_r;Y_1,\\ldots,Y_s)]-\\sum_iT(\\alpha_1,\\ldots,\\nabla_X\\alpha_i,\\ldots,\\alpha_r;Y_1,\\ldots,Y_s)-\\sum_jT(\\alpha_1,\\ldots,\\alpha_r;Y_1,\\ldots,\\nabla_XY_j,\\ldots,Y_s)$. In inertial coordinates every component of nabla_X T is X^b partial_b of that component, with no connection coefficients. (c) Properties. nabla is R-bilinear, C^infinity(Omega)-linear in X, satisfies nabla_X(fY) = X(f)Y + f nabla_X Y and the analogous Leibniz rules for tensor fields, is metric compatible (nabla eta = 0, because partial_a eta_{bc} = 0 in every inertial chart), is torsion-free (nabla_X Y - nabla_Y X = [X,Y], def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields and prop-coordinate-formula-for-the-lie-bracket) and has zero curvature (nabla_X nabla_Y Z - nabla_Y nabla_X Z - nabla_{[X,Y]} Z = 0), the last by equality of mixed partial derivatives of the components (thm-young-mixed-partial-theorem). (d) Fields along a curve. If gamma: I -> A is a C^1 curve and W: I -> V is a C^1 field along it (def-vector-field-and-section-along-a-smooth-curve), the covariant derivative of W along gamma is the ordinary V-valued derivative DW/ds := W' (def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral), because the canonical identification T_pA = V is independent of p; consequently parallel transport along any curve is the identity and a field is parallel exactly when it is constant. The derivative (d) is the one used for the acceleration of congruences, for Fermi-Walker transport and for the kinematic decomposition below; the model needs no Christoffel symbols or parallel-transport ODE in this formulation. (e) First-order C1 version. For C1 vector fields X,Y and C1 covector/tensor fields on Omega, the same directional/evaluation definitions are well-defined and have continuous coefficients: in an inertial chart $(\\nabla_XY)^a=X^b\\partial_bY^a$ and each tensor component is differentiated in the same way. The component recovery and subtraction of all argument derivatives remain valid. C1 scalar multiplication satisfies the same first-order Leibniz rules, metric compatibility remains $\\nabla\\eta=0$, and the first-order torsion identity uses the continuous coordinate bracket $[X,Y]^a=X^b\\partial_bY^a-Y^b\\partial_bX^a$. No C1 closure of this bracket or second covariant derivative of arbitrary C1 data is asserted. For C2 vector fields the second derivatives needed for the zero-curvature identity in(c) exist, and that identity follows by equality of the continuous mixed second partials. All original smooth-field properties and the C1 along-curve derivative in(d) are retained.",
        "strategy": "Definition with well-definedness obligations. (i) The directional derivative in (a) is the derivative of the V-valued composite t |-> Y(p+tX(p)); its coordinate expression is the chain rule, and chart independence is the corrected identity X'^b partial'_b Y'^a=Lambda^a_c X^b partial_b Y^c, equivalently inverse-Lambda recovery of the unprimed components, using that inertial transitions are affine (their second derivatives vanish, so no inhomogeneous term appears) and their linear parts are constant. (ii) The extension in(b) subtracts the derivative of every argument, whether vector or covector. In an inertial chart use the constant coordinate basis and constant dual basis; their covariant derivatives vanish, so evaluating the rule on those bases leaves only X acting on each tensor component. For variable arguments the ordinary product rule cancels all their derivatives with the displayed subtractions. This proves the stated coordinate formula and the evaluation derivation rule; the coordinate expression has no Gamma terms because eta is constant and transition matrices are constant in inertial charts. (iii) The properties in (c) are coordinate computations: torsion-freeness is X^b partial_b Y^a - Y^b partial_b X^a = [X,Y]^a, zero curvature is the interchange of mixed partials, and metric compatibility is the constancy of the component matrix eta_{ab}. (iv) In (d), the canonical isomorphism T_pA = V is independent of p, so the covariant derivative along a curve coincides with the ordinary derivative and parallel transport is trivial; this is exactly what makes Fermi-Walker transport below an ordinary linear ODE.         "statement": "Let $(A,V,\\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]], $c>0$, and let $n\\in V$ be future unit, $\\eta(n,n)=-1$, with rest space $n^\\perp$, rest projection $h(v)=v+\\eta(n,v)n$ and norm $|w|=\\sqrt{\\eta(w,w)}$ on $n^\\perp$ as in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\\,(c).\n(a) For every $P$ in the future closed cone $\\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ define the observer energy of $P$ relative to $n$ by $E_n(P):=-c\\,\\eta(P,n)$, the observer spatial momentum by $q_n(P):=h(P)$, and, when $P$ is nonzero future causal, the invariant mass by $m(P):=\\sqrt{-\\eta(P,P)}/c$. For future null $P$ the same formula gives $m(P)=0$.\n(b) If $m>0$ and $P$ is written as $P=mU$ with $U$ future timelike and $\\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ (the four-velocity normalisation of [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]), call $m$ the rest-mass parameter of $P$, $mc^2$ its rest energy and $T_n(P):=E_n(P)-mc^2$ its kinetic energy relative to the observer $n$ and the parameter $m$. The kinetic energy is defined only after $m$ has been fixed, so it is not a function of $P$ and $n$ alone.\n(c) The definition claims no positivity of $E_n$, no inequality or vanishing property of $T_n$, and no physical measurement. Equivalently $\\dot P(s)=(P\\circ\\rho)'(\\tau(s))$, so $\\dot P$ is the derivative of the proper-time parametrised field $P\\circ\\rho$. Since $\\tau'(s)>0$ by [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]], $\\dot P$ is well defined and continuous whenever $P$ is $C^1$.\n(b) If $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant and $U$ the four-velocity of $x$ ([[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]), then $F:=\\dot P$ is called the four-force on the particle; in an inertial frame $F$ has the components of the derivative of the four-momentum with respect to proper time.\n(c) This item introduces a derivative and a name only.         "statement": "Let $(A,V,\\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski model and $c>0$.\n(a) For a finite list $(P_1,\\dots,P_N)$, $N\\ge0$, of vectors of $V$ define the total four-momentum $P_{\\mathrm{tot}}:=\\sum_{i=1}^NP_i$ as the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive group $(V,+)$; the empty sum is $0$.\n(b) If $P_{\\mathrm{tot}}$ is future timelike, define its invariant mass $M:=M(P_{\\mathrm{tot}}):=\\sqrt{-\\eta(P_{\\mathrm{tot}},P_{\\mathrm{tot}})}/c>0$ and its rest energy $Mc^2$; if $P_{\\mathrm{tot}}$ is future null, set $M:=0$ and say that the system has no rest frame. For zero, spacelike or past $P_{\\mathrm{tot}}$ this convention defines no invariant mass.\n(c) A center-of-momentum frame of a nonzero $P_{\\mathrm{tot}}$ is an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ whose first vector satisfies $q_{e_0}(P_{\\mathrm{tot}})=0$, i.e. the total spatial momentum vanishes for the frame's stationary observer; by [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]] this is equivalent to $P_{\\mathrm{tot}}=-\\eta(P_{\\mathrm{tot}},e_0)e_0$, that is, to $P_{\\mathrm{tot}}$ being a positive multiple of $e_0$.\n(d) The invariant mass of a single future timelike vector $P$ coincides with $m(P)$ of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; in particular for $P=mU$ with $\\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ it equals $m$.\n(e) No existence of a center-of-momentum frame, no physical conservation law and no dynamics are asserted by this definition; position, event and simultaneity data do not enter $\\sum_iP_i$, and only the total vector carries the invariant mass.",

        "title": "Existence and uniqueness of the center-of-momentum frame of a future timelike four-momentum",
        "domain": "mathematics",
        "statement": "Let $(A,V,\\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski model, $c>0$, and let $Q$ be a future timelike vector with invariant mass $M:=\\sqrt{-\\eta(Q,Q)}/c$; put $n_Q:=Q/(Mc)$, so that $\\eta(n_Q,n_Q)=-1$, $n_Q\\in C^+$ and $Q=Mc\\,n_Q$.\n(a) There exists an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $e_0=n_Q$; in every such frame $q_{e_0}(Q)=0$, $E_{e_0}(Q)=Mc^2$ and the components of $Q$ are $(Mc,0,0,0)$. Such a frame is a center-of-momentum frame of $Q$ in the sense of [[def-sr-total-four-momentum-and-invariant-mass]]\\,(c).\n(b) Conversely, if an inertial frame satisfies $q_{e_0}(Q)=0$, then $e_0=n_Q$. Hence the time vector of a center-of-momentum frame of $Q$ is unique, and two center-of-momentum frames of $Q$ differ only by the choice of origin and by a positively oriented $\\eta$-orthonormal change of the spatial basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $n_Q^\\perp$; in particular the center-of-momentum frame is unique up to spatial rotations.\n(c) If $Q$ is a nonzero future null vector, then no inertial frame satisfies $q_{e_0}(Q)=0$: a nonzero future null vector has no center-of-momentum frame.",
        "strategy": "Existence: $n_Q$ is future unit.         "statement": "Adopt as physical assumptions of the relativistic particle model, on top of the flat spacetime model, the ideal-clock and ideal-light postulates and the SI unit conventions: (i) Mass and momentum. Let a massive particle have constant mass $m>0$, four-momentum $P=mU$ and a future unit observer $n$. Its measured energy $E_n(P)=-c\\eta(P,n)$, spatial momentum $q_n(P)=h(P)$ and kinetic energy $T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ satisfy $E_n(P)>0$, $T_n(P)\\ge0$ and the mass-shell identity $E_n(P)^2=m^2c^4+c^2|q_n(P)|^2$; $T_n(P)=0$ if and only if the particle is at rest in the observer's frame ($U=cn$). In an inertial frame whose stationary observer is $n=e_0$, the components are $P=(E/c,\\mathbf p)$ with $E=E_{e_0}(P)=m\\gamma_wc^2$ and $\\mathbf p=q_{e_0}(P)=m\\gamma_w\\mathbf w$ for the coordinate velocity $\\mathbf w$, and under a passive boost the components transform as the components of the vector $P$; the combination $E^2-c^2|\\mathbf p|^2=m^2c^4$ is frame-independent.\n(b) Four-force. Along a $C^2$ worldline with four-acceleration $A$, the four-force $F=\\dot P$ satisfies $\\eta(P,F)=0$ and $F=mA$; in an inertial frame $F=\\gamma\\,(\\mathbf f\\cdot\\mathbf w/c,\\mathbf f)$ and $dE/dt=\\mathbf f\\cdot\\mathbf w$, where $\\mathbf f=d\\mathbf p/dt$ is the coordinate three-force. The constancy of $m$ is used; if instead $m$ is a $C^1$ variable mass parameter, then $\\eta(P,F)=-mc^2\\,dm/d\\tau$, and the constant-mass identities are not transferred to variable-mass systems.\n(c) System mass. For a finite nonempty system of particles all of whose four-momenta are nonzero future causal and whose total four-momentum $Q$ is future timelike, the invariant mass $M=\\sqrt{-\\eta(Q,Q)}/c$ satisfies: in the center-of-momentum frame with $e_0=Q/(Mc)$ one has $Mc^2=\\sum_iE_{e_0}(P_i)$; every massive constituent has $E_{e_0}(P_i)\\ge m_ic^2$, with equality exactly when it is at rest in that frame, and every massless constituent has $E_{e_0}(P_i)>0$. Hence $M\\ge\\sum_im_i$ over the massive constituents, with equality if and only if the system is massive-only and all its constituents are at rest in the center-of-momentum frame. Let $M$ be the invariant mass of the common total four-momentum $Q$ when $Q$ is future timelike. Then the necessary inequalities $M\\ge\\sum_im_i$ and $M\\ge\\sum_j\\mu_j$ hold; if the incoming side is a projectile of mass $m_1$ and a target of mass $m_2$ at rest in the observer frame of the target, with projectile energy $E$ and kinetic energy $T=E-m_1c^2$ in that frame, then\n$$E\\ \\ge\\ \\frac{c^2}{2m_2}\\Bigl[\\Bigl(\\sum_{j=1}^K\\mu_j\\Bigr)^2-m_1^2-m_2^2\\Bigr],\\qquad T\\ \\ge\\ \\frac{c^2}{2m_2}\\Bigl[\\Bigl(\\sum_{j=1}^K\\mu_j\\Bigr)^2-(m_1+m_2)^2\\Bigr],$$\nand a single incoming massless particle cannot collide into an outgoing state containing a massive particle. These are kinematic necessity statements under the adopted conservation: they do not assert that any collision occurs, do not fix probabilities, amplitudes or cross sections, and are not empirical findings.\n(f) Scope.
